main_skill: Manage multiple patients: rapid assessment, triage/prioritization, treatment order, changing conditions
core_question: Who needs attention first among many patients?

protocol_reference.usage_note: The TRIAGE_SWEEP decisions follow the START flow: can the patient walk? -> is the patient breathing (after airway repositioning if needed)? -> respiratory rate above/below 30? -> perfusion (radial pulse / capillary refill)? -> mental status (obeys commands)? Categories: IMMEDIATE (red), DELAYED (yellow), MINOR (green), EXPECTANT (black/grey).

protocol_reference.attribution: CDC MMWR Guidelines for Field Triage of Injured Patients
protocol_reference.usage_note: Treatment-order and resource-allocation decisions after triage follow CDC field-triage logic: physiologic criteria (airway, breathing, circulation, mental status) determine who is transported/treated first among multiple IMMEDIATE patients.

note: All names, vitals, and clinical details below are entirely fictional training content generated for simulation purposes. This scenario depicts a fictional mass-casualty incident (multi-vehicle bus collision) for emergency-triage training only.
scope_note: Given 6 simultaneous patients, each carries one triage decision plus one condensed management decision (rather than the 4-decision depth used for single-patient Level 1) so the level remains playable within a mass-casualty time pressure window. Every decision still offers 4 fully-branched options with distinct consequences.

dialogue: Doctor, a multi-vehicle bus collision just brought in six patients at once.
We don't have time to fully examine everyone. We need to triage fast and treat in the right order.
I'll call out each patient as they come in -- tell me their triage category and then how we manage them.

TRIAGE_SWEEP.instruction: Assign a START triage category to each of the 6 patients before treatment begins. Each patient is its own decision node below; the engine should present them together as one rapid-fire sweep.

nurse_dialogue: Vikram can't walk -- he's pinned and bleeding, breathing fast at 32, and his radial pulse is weak.
What's his triage category?

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- RR over 30 with weak perfusion.
options.protocol_alignment: START: RR>30 = Immediate
options.consequence: Correctly flagged for first-wave resource allocation.

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- he's talking, so he can wait.
options.protocol_alignment: Ignores RR>30 criterion; a talking patient can still be physiologically Immediate
options.consequence: Vikram's leg bleeding continues untreated for longer than it should; he deteriorates toward hypovolemic shock before reassessment.

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- his injury is only to one limb.
options.protocol_alignment: Ignores respiratory rate and perfusion signs entirely
options.consequence: Severe misclassification -- Vikram is left in the minor-injuries area and continues bleeding unmonitored.

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- his injuries look too severe to save.
options.protocol_alignment: Incorrect use of the expectant category; Vikram is breathing, has a pulse, and is salvageable
options.consequence: A salvageable patient is wrongly deprioritized out of active care.

nurse_dialogue: Ananya walked in herself with a cut arm. She's alert and talking normally.
What's her triage category?

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- ambulatory with a stable, isolated injury.
options.protocol_alignment: START: able to walk = Minor
options.consequence: Correctly directed to the minor-treatment area, freeing bay capacity for higher-acuity patients.

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- any visible bleeding should be Red.
options.protocol_alignment: Over-triage; ties up a trauma bay for a walking, stable patient
options.consequence: A trauma bay is occupied unnecessarily while Immediate patients wait.

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- she'll need stitches eventually.
options.protocol_alignment: Minor over-triage; she qualifies as Minor, not Delayed
options.consequence: Minor over-triage; not dangerous, but slightly inefficient use of the delayed queue.

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- deprioritize since she is stable.
options.protocol_alignment: Severe misuse of the expectant category for a stable walking patient
options.consequence: Alarming misclassification; would abandon a clearly salvageable, low-acuity patient.

nurse_dialogue: Deepak wasn't breathing at all, Doctor. After we repositioned his airway, he started breathing again -- shallow, about 8 a minute.
What's his triage category?

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- breathes only after airway repositioning.
options.protocol_alignment: START: apneic patient who breathes after repositioning = Immediate
options.consequence: Correctly flagged as the highest priority for airway management and resuscitation.

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- he wasn't breathing, so he's not salvageable.
options.protocol_alignment: Misapplies Expectant; per START, breathing after repositioning is a defining feature of Immediate, not Expectant
options.consequence: A salvageable patient with an obstructed airway is wrongly written off.

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- he's breathing now, so he can wait.
options.protocol_alignment: Ignores that breathing only resumed after intervention -- a hallmark Immediate criterion
options.consequence: His shallow breathing goes unmanaged and he deteriorates toward respiratory arrest again.

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- he's breathing on his own now.
options.protocol_alignment: Severe misclassification of a patient who required airway intervention to breathe at all
options.consequence: Critical delay in reaching a patient who needs immediate airway support.

nurse_dialogue: Priya is 8. She won't follow simple commands and seems confused, but her injuries look minor.
What's her triage category?

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- fails the mental status / obeys-commands check.
options.protocol_alignment: START: altered mental status (does not obey commands) = Immediate, regardless of visible injury severity
options.consequence: Correctly prioritized -- her delayed capillary refill and confusion suggest evolving shock or head injury that visible injuries alone would miss.

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- her visible injuries are minor.
options.protocol_alignment: Ignores the mental-status criterion entirely, the most sensitive marker in a pediatric patient
options.consequence: A deteriorating pediatric patient is left unmonitored in the minor area.

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- she can wait since she's not bleeding heavily.
options.protocol_alignment: Misses the altered-mental-status Immediate criterion
options.consequence: Delayed recognition of a likely head injury or shock state in a child.

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- confusion suggests a severe untreatable injury.
options.protocol_alignment: Wildly premature use of the expectant category on a breathing, pulse-present child
options.consequence: Serious misclassification; she is fully salvageable with prompt care.

nurse_dialogue: Ravi has chest wall pain and can't walk because of it, but he's breathing normally, has a good pulse, and is answering questions clearly.
What's his triage category?

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- normal RR, present pulse, obeys commands, but cannot walk.
options.protocol_alignment: START: normal breathing/perfusion/mental status but non-ambulatory = Delayed
options.consequence: Correctly placed in the Delayed queue -- monitored, but not competing with Immediate patients for the first wave of resources.

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- chest pain always means Immediate.
options.protocol_alignment: Over-triage; his physiologic criteria (RR, perfusion, mental status) all meet Delayed thresholds
options.consequence: A trauma bay and scarce first-wave resources are consumed by a physiologically stable patient.

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- he's stable, so treat him like a walking wounded.
options.protocol_alignment: Ignores that he cannot walk, the key criterion excluding Minor
options.consequence: He is placed with ambulatory patients despite being unable to walk, risking him being overlooked.

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- his age puts him at higher risk.
options.protocol_alignment: Age is not a START criterion; this misclassifies a stable, salvageable patient
options.consequence: Inappropriate and unjustified deprioritization.

nurse_dialogue: Suresh isn't breathing, Doctor, even after we repositioned his airway. No pulse either.
What's his triage category?

options.text: EXPECTANT (Black/Grey) -- apneic and pulseless despite airway repositioning.
options.protocol_alignment: START: remains apneic after repositioning = Expectant in a resource-constrained MCI
options.consequence: Correctly and difficultly categorized; resources are preserved for salvageable patients, and comfort-focused care is arranged for Suresh where possible.

options.text: IMMEDIATE (Red) -- attempt full resuscitation regardless of resource strain.
options.protocol_alignment: In a true MCI with overwhelmed resources, START directs personnel away from patients who remain apneic after repositioning, to save the greatest number of salvageable patients overall
options.consequence: Diverts the team's only spare hands from three other Immediate patients who are still salvageable, at significant cost to overall survival.

options.text: DELAYED (Yellow) -- reassess him again in a few minutes.
options.protocol_alignment: Miscategorization -- he does not meet any Delayed criteria
options.consequence: Wastes time that should go to salvageable patients without changing his outcome.

options.text: MINOR (Green) -- skip him and move on without any categorization.
options.protocol_alignment: Fails to formally record his status, which affects the incident log and family communication
options.consequence: No immediate clinical harm, but creates confusion in the incident record.

evaluator.note: START triage is designed to take under 30 seconds per patient in real practice; the 8-second target reflects the compressed pace of the simulation.

nurse_dialogue: We have three IMMEDIATE patients now: Vikram, Deepak, and Priya. We only have enough hands to fully manage them one at a time before the next ambulance crew arrives to help.
What order do you want to treat them in?

options.text: Deepak first (airway is the most immediately life-threatening problem), then Priya (evolving shock/head injury), then Vikram (ongoing but currently controllable bleeding).
options.protocol_alignment: CDC field-triage logic: airway compromise takes precedence over evolving-but-currently-compensated shock and controllable external hemorrhage
options.consequence: All three IMMEDIATE patients receive timely care in physiologically sound order.

options.text: Vikram first (visible bleeding is most alarming), then Deepak, then Priya.
options.protocol_alignment: Prioritizes visible bleeding over an unmanaged airway problem, which is a higher physiologic threat
options.consequence: Deepak's shallow breathing goes unsupported for longer, risking a second respiratory arrest while Vikram's bleeding -- already partly controlled by a pressure dressing -- is treated first.

options.text: Priya first (she's a child), then Vikram, then Deepak.
options.protocol_alignment: Prioritizes by age/emotional salience rather than physiologic threat; Deepak's airway is the more time-critical problem
options.consequence: Deepak deteriorates further while airway support is delayed.

options.text: Treat whichever patient is closest, without applying any prioritization logic.
options.protocol_alignment: No physiologic prioritization applied
options.consequence: Random treatment order leads to unpredictable, and on average worse, outcomes across the three patients.

nurse_dialogue: Deepak's airway is our first priority, Doctor. What would you like to do?

options.text: Insert an airway adjunct, provide bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen, and reassess breathing continuously.
nurse_response: He's oxygenating better, Doctor. Airway secured for transport.

options.text: Leave him on his back without repositioning and move to the next patient.
nurse_response: Doctor, he's stopped breathing again -- we lost the airway.

options.text: Wait for the second ambulance crew to arrive before doing anything.
nurse_response: Doctor, we can't wait -- his airway needs attention now.

options.text: Focus only on IV fluids without addressing the airway.
nurse_response: Doctor, fluids won't help if he can't breathe -- his airway needed to come first.

nurse_dialogue: Priya's confusion hasn't improved, and her capillary refill is still slow, Doctor. What would you like to do?

options.text: Secure IV access, give a fluid bolus for suspected compensated shock, apply oxygen, and prepare for urgent imaging once stabilized.
nurse_response: She's more responsive now, Doctor -- following simple commands again.

options.text: Assume the confusion is just fear and offer reassurance only.
nurse_response: Doctor, she's becoming less responsive -- this wasn't just fear.

options.text: Send her for a full-body CT scan immediately without stabilizing her first.
nurse_response: Doctor, she deteriorated in the scanner -- she needed stabilizing first.

options.text: Move her to the minor-injuries area since her external injuries look small.
nurse_response: Doctor, she's not safe in the minor area -- she needed monitoring.

nurse_dialogue: Vikram's leg is still bleeding, Doctor. What would you like to do?

options.text: Apply a tourniquet above the wound, secure IV access, give fluids, and prepare for urgent orthopedic/surgical handover.
nurse_response: Bleeding's controlled, Doctor. He's ready for the surgical team.

options.text: Apply a simple gauze dressing without pressure and move on.
nurse_response: Doctor, the bleeding hasn't stopped -- he's getting paler.

options.text: Wait for X-ray results before addressing the bleeding.
nurse_response: Doctor, we can't wait on imaging -- the bleeding needs to be controlled now.

options.text: Use both remaining tourniquets on him 'to be safe', even though one is sufficient.
nurse_response: Bleeding's controlled, Doctor, but now we have no tourniquets left for anyone else.

nurse_dialogue: Ravi's still stable but in pain and can't walk, Doctor. What would you like to do for him in the Delayed queue?

options.text: Give appropriate analgesia, place on a spinal board for safe transfer, and reassess vitals every few minutes while Immediate patients are managed.
nurse_response: He's more comfortable, Doctor, and ready for transfer when a bay opens up.

options.text: Leave him completely unattended until every Immediate patient is finished.
nurse_response: He's still stable, Doctor, but in a lot of pain from waiting so long.

options.text: Pull a trauma bay and full monitoring resources for him despite his Delayed status.
nurse_response: He's comfortable, Doctor, but that trauma bay was needed for an Immediate patient.

options.text: Send him home to rest since he is talking normally.
nurse_response: Doctor, he collapsed at home -- his rib injury needed proper evaluation before discharge.

nurse_dialogue: Ananya's laceration is still oozing, Doctor. What would you like to do for her in the Minor queue?

options.text: Clean and dress the wound, check tetanus status, and arrange suturing once an Immediate/Delayed bay is free.
nurse_response: Wound's dressed and clean, Doctor. She's comfortable waiting for suturing.

options.text: Ignore her entirely until every other patient is fully finished.
nurse_response: She's stable, Doctor, but her wound is still open and at risk of infection the longer it waits.

options.text: Pull a trauma bay and continuous monitoring for her despite her Minor status.
nurse_response: She's fine, Doctor, but that bay was needed elsewhere.

options.text: Discharge her immediately without dressing the wound or checking tetanus status.
nurse_response: Doctor, she came back later with an infected wound -- we should have dressed it properly before she left.

nurse_dialogue: Suresh has been categorized Expectant, Doctor. How do you want to handle him given how stretched we are?

options.text: Assign him brief, dignified comfort measures where possible, document his status clearly, and keep the team's active resources focused on the salvageable Immediate patients.
options.protocol_alignment: Standard MCI practice: Expectant patients receive comfort-focused attention without diverting scarce active-resuscitation resources from salvageable patients
nurse_response: Understood, Doctor. I'll note his status and check on him between the other patients.

options.text: Commit the team's only spare hands to full resuscitation on him for as long as it takes.
options.protocol_alignment: Diverts limited personnel from salvageable Immediate patients in a true resource-overwhelmed MCI, reducing overall survivors
nurse_response: Doctor, while we were with him, Priya's condition worsened without anyone watching her.

options.text: Leave him completely unattended and undocumented.
options.protocol_alignment: Fails the documentation and dignity expectations of MCI protocol even when active resuscitation is not appropriate
nurse_response: Doctor, the incident log has no record for him -- his family will need an answer later.

options.text: Move him to the Minor-injuries area to avoid confronting the situation.
options.protocol_alignment: Mislabels and mismanages an Expectant patient, creating confusion in the triage area
nurse_response: Doctor, that's caused confusion in the minor area -- we need to correct his placement.

flow_control.explanation: No decision node's option points directly at another patient's decision node -- every node here is a self-contained single decision (or, for TRIAGE_SWEEP, one decision per patient within that sweep). The engine advances between patients/nodes ONLY by following the fixed sequence below, never by an embedded next_decision cross-reference. After each decision, the engine presents the SAME patient's next node if one exists (none do at this level's depth -- see scope_note), otherwise it advances to the next step in this sequence.

sequence.on_complete: the option chosen here sets the order for steps 8-10 among P3_MANAGEMENT, P4_MANAGEMENT and P1_MANAGEMENT; option A's order (P3, P4, P1) is used below by default

endings.level_outcome_logic: Level 4 result is computed across all 6 patients. SUCCESS requires: (1) correct or acceptable START category chosen for at least 5 of 6 patients, (2) no patient in P1_MANAGEMENT, P3_MANAGEMENT, or P4_MANAGEMENT reaching CRITICAL_ENDPOINT, and (3) P5 and P2 reaching a STABLE_* status. Any Immediate patient reaching CRITICAL_ENDPOINT triggers overall level FAILURE.

SUCCESS_WITH_PENALTY.banner: MASS CASUALTY EVENT MANAGED (RESOURCE-INEFFICIENT / TRIAGE ERRORS)

FAILURE.banner: MASS CASUALTY EVENT - PREVENTABLE LOSS OF LIFE

performance_report_schema.treatment_order_accuracy: boolean - whether TREATMENT_ORDER option A was selected
